points.description: Reduction/setup: assumes for contradiction that all roots of P are real (distinct), and reduces to the case n=k+1 (or otherwise sets up divisors of degree k as products of linear factors, i.e. P divided by a single root factor when n=k+1). Equivalent valid setups accepted.

Proves that two different divisors of P (of degree k) share the position of a zero coefficient (e.g. by showing that the divisors P/(x-r_i) each must have some zero coefficient, and a pigeonhole/sign-pattern argument forces two different divisors to have a zero at the same index).

Uses this to derive that a polynomial with only distinct real roots has two consecutive zero coefficients (or an equivalent forbidden configuration, obtained e.g. from the difference/combination of the two divisors).

Obtains the contradiction: a real-rooted polynomial with distinct roots cannot have two consecutive zero coefficients (e.g. via Rolle's theorem/derivatives or Descartes-type argument), so P must have a non-real root. Conclusion stated clearly.

rubric.notes: Full marks for a complete, correct proof by any valid method. Partial credit: proving that two divisors share a zero-coefficient position (with the n=k+1 reduction), or finding a real-rooted distinct-root polynomial having two consecutive zero coefficients, earns the corresponding points. Minor errors in an otherwise complete proof lose only a mark or so.
